caption_gt: H&E-stained section (100x) showing histopathological features suggestive of intramucosal nevi. The image displays the proliferation of nevus cells, characterized by cohesive islands of polygonal to oval epithelioid cells with focal melanin pigment production. Nests of nevus cells are separated by a hyalinised band beneath the stratified squamous surface epithelium. The nevus cells exhibit junctional separation and differentiation, without significant cellular atypia or dysplasia. The associated fibrous connective tissue contains dense bundles of collagen fibres. A yellow arrow points to Type A cells, which are large and round, without dendritic processes, located at the periphery adjacent to the epithelium with intense melanin accumulation. A blue arrow points to Type B cells, which are uniform, round to polygonal, found in deeper layers, and show decreased melanin deposition. Lesional cells are observed close to the excision borders.

caption_gt: Histopathologic features of keratoacanthoma, observed at 40× magnification. This image, stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E), illustrates characteristic features of keratoacanthoma across its various developmental and regressive phases. The early proliferation phase of keratoacanthoma is characterized by a small, primarily solid tumor containing several distinct infundibulocystic structures that have not yet coalesced into a central keratin plug. These structures include islands of laminated keratin with a ground-glass appearance, which may merge. Nuclear atypia is typically absent within the center of these structures, though some peripheral atypia may be allowed, and generally becomes less prominent with maturation. Inflammation, involving histiocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils, and plasma cells, may also be present. The maturation phase demonstrates more defined features, such as an exo–endophytic squamous proliferation with a central keratin plug, overhanging epithelial lips, and compact keratinization. Significant variability of cellular appearance and atypia can be observed, with most pleomorphic cells located in the most distant fringes. The regression phase presents with a “hollowing out” of the lesion, losing its central keratin plug, and beginning to resemble an empty bowl as the keratin clears and the epithelium thins. This phase is also marked by perilesional dermal inflammation, particularly lymphocytic infiltrate, and increasing cicatricial fibrosis.

caption_gt: Histopathologic features of keratoacanthoma, observed at 100× magnification. This image, stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E), illustrates characteristic features of keratoacanthoma across its various developmental and regressive phases. The early proliferation phase of keratoacanthoma is characterized by a small, primarily solid tumor containing several distinct infundibulocystic structures that have not yet coalesced into a central keratin plug. These structures include islands of laminated keratin with a ground-glass appearance, which may merge. Nuclear atypia is typically absent within the center of these structures, though some peripheral atypia may be allowed, and generally becomes less prominent with maturation. Inflammation, involving histiocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils, and plasma cells, may also be present. The maturation phase demonstrates more defined features, such as an exo–endophytic squamous proliferation with a central keratin plug, overhanging epithelial lips, and compact keratinization. Significant variability of cellular appearance and atypia can be observed, with most pleomorphic cells located in the most distant fringes. The regression phase presents with a “hollowing out” of the lesion, losing its central keratin plug, and beginning to resemble an empty bowl as the keratin clears and the epithelium thins. This phase is also marked by perilesional dermal inflammation, particularly lymphocytic infiltrate, and increasing cicatricial fibrosis.

caption_gt: Histopathology of Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) stained with hematoxylin and eosin (HE) at ×400 magnification. The image displays sheets, trabeculae, and cords of small monomorphic round blue cells with large nuclei and small amounts of cytoplasm. Nuclei exhibit fine granular/clear chromatin, indistinct nucleoli, and numerous mitoses. Consistent with standard hematoxylin-eosin staining of skin MCC biopsies, these cells show scant cytoplasm and abundant mitoses. The small basophilic tumoral cells are arranged in sheets, nests, and ribbons, separated by stroma, frequently forming nodules. Mitotic figures are a common histological feature, crucial for diagnosing and differentiating this tumor from other malignancies.

caption_gt: Histopathology of Melasma (400×, H&E). A higher power examination of the papillary dermis highlights pigment-laden macrophages (dermal melanophages) and intermixed solar elastosis. Dermal melanophages are formed when melanin, having seeped into the dermis due to basement membrane disruption, is phagocytosed by macrophages. These are particularly common in dermal and mixed types of melasma. Solar elastosis, a hallmark of chronic sun damage, is also observed and characterized by the accumulation of abnormal elastic fibers, indicative of UV-induced skin aging.

caption_gt: Histological image (hematoxylin-eosin, 10× magnification) of an NRAS- and CCND1 gene-mutated melanoma, 4.9 mm-thick with a mitotic rate of 11/mm², from the forearm of an 80-year-old woman. The image displays dilated capillaries (arrows) located beneath the epidermis and extending between tumor dermal aggregates. These dilated capillaries are a histological manifestation of the vascular patterns seen dermoscopically and are significantly associated with mutations in cell cycle genes like CCND1. This neoangiogenesis reflects the tumor's adaptive response to the increasing oxygen and nutrient demands of rapidly proliferating melanoma cells, often under hypoxic conditions, leading to the activation of factors like HIF-1α that induce the expression of genes involved in angiogenesis and melanoma progression.

caption_gt: Histopathology of nodular melanoma, stained with hematoxylin-eosin at 10× magnification. The image displays a densely packed dermal proliferation of atypical melanocytes extending to the reticular dermis, consistent with Clark’s level IV and a Breslow thickness of 2.9 mm. Several dermal mitoses are evident, counted at 10 mitoses per 1 mm². Nodular melanoma lesions frequently exhibit such dermal mitosis and may also present with epidermal ulceration. Histologically, a key diagnostic feature for nodular melanoma is that if an intraepidermal component is present, it should not extend for more than three rete ridges beyond the dermal component.

caption_gt: Histopathology (hematoxylin-eosin stain, 10× magnification) showing superficial spreading melanoma infiltrating the superficial dermis, with a Breslow thickness of 0.7 mm. The melanoma exhibits moderate non-brisk peritumoral and intratumoral inflammatory infiltrate. Histologically, superficial spreading melanoma is characterized by asymmetric, poorly demarcated melanocytes that lack cellular maturation. Melanocytes are distributed unevenly, often with solitary melanocytes being more predominant over nests, and commonly with evidence of intraepithelial spread in a pagetoid manner.

caption_gt: High-power photomicrograph showing pathologic findings consistent with congenital melanocytic nevi, stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). The image displays the keratinized, stratified squamous epithelium (thick black arrow) and the epidermodermal junction (thick white arrow). The epidermis is thinned out with loss of rete pegs. The underlying dermis shows diffuse deposition of melanin pigment (thin white arrow) and the presence of melanocytes (thin black arrow) around and within the hair follicles. These findings, observed during microscopic examination of the patient's scalp swelling, also included lobules and nests of nevi cells, hair follicles, sweat glands, and sebaceous glands, with melanin pigment and melanocytes extending up to the deep subcutis and infiltrating the fat, all indicative of congenital melanocytic nevi.

caption_gt: Photomicrographic image of a cross-section of the entire resected fistula piece, stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) at 2× magnification. This image shows the fistulous tract, the lentiginous melanocytic hyperplasia, and the perianal skin epidermis. The melanoma, which was quite small and found incidentally during histological examination, is located in the depth of the subcutaneous tissue, next to the fistulous tract, the interior of which was already epithelialised. The melanoma is surrounded by an abundant inflammatory response and is next to the visible lesion showing atypical lentiginous melanocytic hyperplasia. The presence of lentiginous hyperplasia suggested that the melanocytic lesion originated inside the fistulous tract, supporting the diagnosis of a primary melanoma. The opening of the fistulous tract in the perianal skin epidermis does not contain signs of inflammation or malignant tissue, ruling out the possibility of the fistula being a complication or a secondary manifestation of a cutaneous melanoma.
